newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa FinMin welcomes Malaysia TA Bank.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa FinMin welcomes Malaysia TA Bank.

text.p: South Africa's Finance Minister Trevor Manuel on Tuesday welcomed Malaysia's TA Bank to the local banking fold as it opened its doors -- the eleventh foreign bank to do so with a full South African banking license. "This event marks a milestone in the economic and trade relationships between South Africa and Malaysia," Manuel said in notes prepared for delivery.

TA Bank joins the dozens of foreign banks that have entered the South African market since the first democratic elections in 1994, either as fully licensed operations or one of 58 representative offices, stealing business away from local players.
TA Bank is a unit of Malaysian stockbroking and finance group TA Enterprise Bhd which first entered South Africa early last year when it brought local stockbrokers Kilroe Whitehead.

Manuel noted the financial services sector had attracted the greatest number of foreign investors to South Africa since 1994, when the country amended legislation to allow foreign banks to set up shop here under the same constraints as locals.
"TA Bank had no problems meeting the criteria -- with a 150 million rand ($33 million) investment in capital...and they intend increasing this to 500 million ($110 million) in five years," he added.
The bank's capital investment was three times the minimum legal requirement to begin operating in South Africa, the minister said.

TA Enterprise executive chairman Datuk Tony Tiah said in a separate statement that his group was optimistic about sub-Saharan Africa's growth prospects and was looking at opening representative offices in South Africa's neighbouring countries.

TA Bank aimed to offer financing services to South African clients trading with the southeast Asian region as well as providing traditional banking services to mid-sized corporate and commercial clients.
Manuel said he hoped TA Bank would help reverse South Africa's poor saving culture by encouraging its clients to put away money.
He said in the 15 days since South Africa loosened individual exchange controls, the country's reserves had not been hit by a sudden capital outflow and business confidence had improved as a result.
On July 1 Pretoria raised the offshore investment threshold for indivuals to 200,000 rand ($44,000).
Malaysia was ranked as South Africa's second biggest investor in a recent survey by BusinessMap.
